question: Why do fast-charging claims so often stop at 80%, not 100%?
answer: Because the last fifth is slow by design. A charger pushes full current until the cell hits its voltage limit, often near 80%, then holds that voltage while the current fades, as a nearly full anode takes lithium in slowly. On a long drive, two stops to 80% usually beat one to 100%.
move: When a figure stops at a round number, ask what happens after it.
ask: Which number do I trust that stops at a round figure, and what happens after it?

start.text: The ad says: fast charge to 80%. It never says 100%.

levels.text: The last fifth can take as long as the first four fifths.
Near full, the charger stops pushing and holds the voltage steady.
A nearly full anode has few free slots, so lithium queues to get in.
Rush it, and lithium plates out as metal that wears the cell.

options: Lithium queues at a full anode

reference: Reddy (ed.), Linden's Handbook of Batteries, 4th edition, McGraw-Hill, 2011
